headline: Caribbean Scientists Map Hidden Ocean Depths Off Trinidad and Tobago
meta_description: A milestone expedition led by Caribbean researchers documents uncharted deep-sea waters, discovering dozens of new species and complex ecosystems.
summary_short: Caribbean scientists conducted the region's most comprehensive deep-sea survey, mapping 11,335 square kilometers and collecting over 700 specimens believed to include ne…
body:
In a historic milestone for Caribbean science, a predominantly Caribbean research team recently completed one of the most comprehensive deep-sea surveys ever undertaken in Trinidad and Tobago's waters. Led by deep-sea ecologist Diva Amon, a Trinidad and Tobago native, the month-long expedition aboard the R/V Falkor mapped 11,335 square kilometers of previously uncharted seafloor—an area roughly two-and-a-half times the size of Grand Canyon National Park. The team collected over 700 specimens, with many expected to be identified as new species, including a likely-new octopus of the genus Graneledone. Most significantly, this marks the first time a predominantly Caribbean team has led deep-ocean exploration in the region, breaking what Amon calls the pattern of "parachute science" that has long dominated the field.

Beyond the species discoveries, the expedition revealed 25 active cold seep ecosystems—complex environments formed by methane and other gases rising from the ocean floor. Some stretched across vast areas; one ecosystem sprawled over roughly a square kilometer, teeming with mussels and tube worms. The team's footage captured remarkable moments: a black swallower fish with a stomach grotesquely distended from swallowing prey larger than itself, and a Mobula ray carcass on the seafloor surrounded by feeding crabs and worms. All collected specimens will eventually be housed in the Zoology Museum at the University of the West Indies in Trinidad and Tobago, increasing the museum's deep-sea collection by twelve times over.

Amon hopes the expedition's findings will inform decision-makers in Trinidad and Tobago about protecting these waters from oil and gas drilling, plastic pollution, and climate change. As marine scientist La Daana Kanhai noted, every sample provides "evidence-based decision-making" for the nation's marine stewardship—transforming scientific discovery into practical conservation.
quick_facts: Led by Diva Amon, a Trinidad and Tobago native and deep-sea ecologist
Mapped 11,335 square kilometers of previously uncharted seafloor in one month
Collected over 700 specimens, including at least 20 believed to be new species
Identified 25 active cold seep ecosystems formed by methane and other gases
First predominantly Caribbean-led deep-ocean exploration team in the Caribbean region
